outcomes: Checks that a weak enemy pawn exists before planning a regrouping
Counts the enemy attackers of the stepping square before regrouping through it
Chooses a regrouping that heads for a square from which the target can be attacked, not a move that only waits
Sees when no regrouping is needed or possible
sources: content/items/lesson-ds511.json (positions from Lichess standard rated games, January 2013 sample, CC0; failing twins are one-piece edits marked authored)

steps.text: The lesson *Manoeuvring: a target, a pivot and a route* named the target, the pivot and the route. Here you choose without help. *Rule of thumb:* a regrouping is worth a move when a weak pawn exists, the stepping square is safe, and your pieces have more room than his. The lesson *Who goes, who stays: allocating pieces to a plan* shows how to pick the pieces.

A route often fails if the opponent attacks the stepping square, because he may gain a tempo by chasing the piece; check the attack is real (defended? an exchange you like?). It is pointless with no weak pawn or with a tactic on the board. Count the enemy attackers before you walk. Compare the pair below, which differs by one piece, with a position that has no target.

steps.title: A safe route, an attacked route, no target
steps.prompt: Predict the answer in each position. The first two differ by one piece: name it and the square it attacks. In the third, say why the rule of thumb does not govern the position.

Paper exercise (the app does not check it): in a quiet position from one of your games, write the target, the stepping square and how many enemy pieces attack it. Then write two moves that would only wait, and say why the regrouping is better than either.
